planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in cool, moist, peaty or mineral soil once the ground is workable; this circumboreal shrub resists extreme winter cold but struggles in hot, humid summers.

directions: This low, twiggy shrub forms slow-spreading thickets of small, rounded, coarsely toothed leaves that color bronze-yellow in autumn across tundra, moorland, and alpine habitats of the Northern Hemisphere. It tolerates thin, acidic, or boggy soils where larger trees fail, making it a reliable choice for rock gardens, troughs, and cold-climate native plantings. Give it an open site with good light and avoid competing with aggressive neighbors, since it spreads gradually by underground runners rather than fast top growth. Winter interest comes from fine reddish-brown twigs rather than showy bark.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Sow fresh acorns an inch deep right after fall collection; they need no stratification and sprout readily the following spring. Thin or transplant seedlings while the taproot is still shallow.

directions: A common woodland oak of Japan, Korea, and China, this species bears glossy, coarsely toothed leaves and small acorns in shallow, scaly cups that mature in a single season. It is widely coppiced in its native range for charcoal production and is a favorite subject for bonsai and Japanese garden design because of its tidy branching habit and attractive peeling gray-brown bark on older trunks. Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic soil and give it room to develop its broad, rounded crown; fall color is a warm russet-brown. It adapts readily to cultivation outside Asia wherever summers are not excessively hot and humid.

planting.note: Start seed indoors and harden off after frost danger passes; set plants in lean, fast-draining soil since wet winter feet are the main cause of loss in marginal climates.

directions: Native to volcanic slopes of the Canary Islands, this woody-based sage carries large, triangular, white-felted leaves on a bold architectural subshrub. Showy magenta-pink bracts persist well after the small violet flowers fade, giving the summer display unusually long color. It thrives on neglect in hot, dry gardens and coastal plantings but needs sharp drainage to survive winter wet. Cut back hard in early spring to keep the loose, sprawling habit tidy and encourage fresh felted growth.

planting.note: Start seed indoors with a cold period to improve germination, or propagate by division of established crowns; set out in lean, gritty, free-draining soil.

directions: Native to the steppes of central and eastern Europe and Russia, this clump-forming sage sends up wiry, arching stems topped with one-sided racemes of violet-blue flowers that nod gracefully to one side, unlike the stiffly upright spikes of most garden salvias. The grey-green basal foliage stays low and tidy, making it a good front-of-border choice in dry gravel gardens. It resents rich, damp soil and overfeeding, performing best where it must struggle a little. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the plant, though the seed heads also have some winter architectural value.
